title: Schools are soccer, not basketball.
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: O'Brien recounts taking over a failing school and assuming it was a talent problem, only to find talented, serious educators stranded in a building with no structure. He borrows the strong-link versus weak-link distinction: basketball is decided by the best player, soccer by the weakest touches, and a school is soccer because a child touches every classroom, adult and handoff. He argues the common sequence of culture first, systems later is backward. He built systems first (visible data, constant leadership presence, relentless coaching, weekly data meetings, a consistently held behavior system), and the trust and loyalty accumulated afterward as a result. Two stories, a veteran teacher who experienced the structure as permission and a literacy coach who finally stepped in, carry the case that conditions, not knowledge, were the constraint.
points: A failing school is usually a weak-link problem: the school performs at the level of its weakest touches, so raising the floor beats collecting stars.
Talent was already in the building; the failure was that nothing connected it to anything else.
Systems before culture: the author's culture was a result that built up on top of running systems, not the starting point.
Consistent structure and predictability can feel like permission, not a cage, to the strongest teachers.
A coach with the right knowledge still needed structure, repetition and safety before she could use it, so conditions rather than knowledge were the constraint.
quotes: Soccer is the opposite. Soccer is a weak-link game. The ball moves through everyone, and so the team is only as good as its weakest touches — the defender who loses his mark, the midfielder who can’t trap a pass under pressure.

A school isn’t basketball. A school is soccer. A kid doesn’t spend the year with my three best teachers; a kid spends it touching everyone — every classroom, every hallway, every adult, every handoff between them.
I believed that. I think most of us believe that. It feels not just correct but kind. It feels like the humane sequence.
That’s the word she’d use later. Permission. All that structure I was nervous would feel like a cage, she experienced as a door finally opening.
The trust didn’t come before the hard changes, softening the runway for them. The trust came because of them.

She was not a different person. She was the same coach, with the same knowledge she’d walked in the door with. What changed was that the system around her had finally given her the structure and the repetition and, most of all, the safety to be the version of herself she’d always been capable of being.

I didn’t build the culture. I built the systems, and the culture was what accumulated on top of them, like residue, once the systems underneath started actually running. The systems were the cause. The culture was the result.
